## the mess

![](phd-desk-entropy.gif){width="60%" fig-align="center" fig-alt="PhD Comics Desk Entropy: a workspace degenerating into clutter as entropy rises over time."}

::: {.smaller}
Workspaces tend toward entropy. **AI without specs climbs the curve faster.**
:::

::: {.tinyfoot}
Comic: Jorge Cham · phdcomics.com (Desk Entropy, 2005)
:::

::: {.notes}
~90s. Merges origin + sprawl + entropy.

- start of my PhD: a dataset from a departing postdoc, no naming convention, changing every session
- couldn't list sessions or find paired files, so I hand-built a DB manager, a batch runner, a tool that emailed me when batches finished (repo PyRatECoG, if asked)
- built a personal lab-ops stack before doing any science; every new analysis meant more
- months later I could not reorient: what is this file, which config produced it; the conventions lived only in my head
- the comic: every project trends to disorder, tidying is temporary
- the new risk: an agent generates files fast, so without specs it adds entropy faster than I remove it
- land it: never doing this by hand again
- then the pivot: with a well-described problem, AI's first win was discovery — it surveys for the best existing tools, so I stop reinventing; the rest of the talk is the specs that hold entropy down
- credit: Jorge Cham, phdcomics.com (Desk Entropy, 2005)
:::

[the folder is the specification: source → raw → derivatives]{.take}

::: {.fragment .qwrap fragment-index=6}
[how can we get derivatives and results **reliably**?]{.bubble}
:::

::: {.tinyfoot}
![](logos/bids.png){height="30px"} meal-prep images adapted from the BIDS Starter Kit · doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.5872274 (CC-BY)
:::

::: {.notes}
~90s. One BIDS slide; the agent transforms source → raw → derivatives.

- BIDS = community standard for how a dataset is laid out; self-describing, so I stop writing bespoke loaders
- the filename carries the metadata (subject / session / datatype); the S is for Specification, a spec keeps a coding agent inside your rules
- modular: source, raw, derivatives kept apart (ingredients, mise en place, the dish); raw stays pristine, derivatives regenerable
- end on the question (bubble): how do we get derivatives reliably? → next slide answers with pipelines
- images adapted from the BIDS Starter Kit (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.5872274, CC-BY)
:::

## Pipelines (Snakemake)

[reconstructed, and never run by hand again]{.take}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="30%"}
::: {.r-stack}
![](let-me-do-that-by-hand.png){width="100%" fig-alt="PhD Comics setup panel: a student thinking 'Let me do that by hand...'"}

![](let-me-do-that-by-hand-frustration.png){.fragment fragment-index=1 width="100%" fig-alt="PhD Comics full strip: the student grows frustrated doing it by hand."}
:::

![](datalad-figs/local_wf.svg){.fragment fragment-index=4 width="92%" fig-align="center" fig-alt="DataLad and git keep every version of data and code; roll back a mistake."}
:::
::: {.column width="22%"}
![](workflow-dag.svg){.fragment fragment-index=2 width="170" fig-align="center" fig-alt="An abstract Snakemake DAG: dataset through rule nodes to results."}
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
![](snakemake-workflow-rules.png){.fragment fragment-index=3 width="98%" fig-align="center" fig-alt="Each colored DAG node is a Snakemake rule with input, output, and a script or shell command."}
:::
:::

::: {.tinyfoot}
![](logos/snakemake.png){height="30px"} ![](logos/datalad.png){height="30px"} Snakemake · DataLad Handbook fig (CC BY-SA) · comic: Jorge Cham, phdcomics.com
:::

::: {.notes}
~2.5 min. Talk the pointers: the manual temptation (comic), then the pipeline (DAG).

- "let me do that by hand" is fine once; across a dataset it is unmaintainable
- the lived case: a chain built by several people, run order forgotten, provenance gone
- I gave the agent the final files, some intermediates, and the loose scripts; it reconstructed which script produced which file and which dependency, and numerically verified by re-running and matching the intermediates
- the colleague who wrote the scripts was surprised; a chat tab cannot do this
- then I locked it into Snakemake: rules declare input/output/params/script; it infers the DAG from filenames and reruns only what is stale
- DataLad + git version data and code; rebuilt a years-old analysis into a reproducible repo, published with the paper
- DAG/automation framing after Köster; comic Jorge Cham (phdcomics.com)
:::

## Exploration, grounded

[the agent, grounded in your code and your literature]{.take}

![](explore-ground.svg){width="90%" fig-align="center" fig-alt="Top: a notebook or script the user and agent edit together. Below, reaching up via skills and MCP: your code (libraries and a search-first skill) and your literature (PDFs through Docling into a searchable corpus)."}

::: {.tinyfoot}
![](logos/marimo.png){height="42px"} Marimo · marimo.io
:::

::: {.notes}
~2 min. The surface is a Marimo notebook or a Python script; the agent's help there is grounded from below.

- grounding cuts hallucination and reinvention: the agent reuses your real implementation, the one that captures the aspects you care about, instead of a naive from-scratch version
- your code, reachable via a skill (search the library first) and an MCP command, even when you have many packages and thin docs
- your literature, reachable via MCP retrieval (RAG): survey how others chose parameters, what algorithms and confounds they report, and get an organized overview
- so the agent gives grounded support, not free-floating guesses
:::

## Publication (Quarto)

[one source; the same results render live into every document]{.take}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="28%"}
![](results-folder.svg){.fragment fragment-index=1 width="100%" fig-alt="A results folder holding a figure, a schematic, and a stats table (mean 4.2, sd, p, n) — the deliverables from the previous slide."}
:::
::: {.column width="8%"}
![](curved-arrow.svg){.fragment fragment-index=2 width="100%" fig-alt="results become one source document"}
:::
::: {.column width="17%"}
![](robot-assemble.svg){.fragment fragment-index=2 width="100%" fig-alt="A robot, fed a SPECS document, assembling the results into one source document."}
:::
::: {.column width="8%"}
![](curved-arrow.svg){.fragment fragment-index=3 width="100%" fig-alt="one source renders into every document"}
:::
::: {.column width="34%"}
![](docs-stack.svg){.fragment fragment-index=3 width="100%" fig-alt="Slides, manuscript, and report — each showing the same live value 4.2."}
:::
:::

::: {.fragment .qwrap fragment-index=4}
[the agent knows the tools; I bring the capability I need and describe what I want]{.bubble .blue}
:::

::: {.tinyfoot}
![](logos/quarto.png){height="30px"} Quarto · quarto.org
:::

::: {.notes}
~75s. The agent takes the results from the last slide and assembles the documents.

- the previous slide left a folder of results: figures, schematics, and the numbers
- the agent, working from your SPECS, assembles them into one source document — code runs and inserts results, stats, and figures inline, no copy-paste
- that one source renders to slides, manuscript, and report; 4.2 is 4.2 everywhere, and change the data and every number updates in sync
- the shift (bubble): I used to spend a long time learning each tool's details; now the agent knows them, so I bring the capabilities I need and a clear description of what I want
- pruning over-generated output is still on me (see the recap's limits box)
:::
